newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - HEALTH AND PENSIONS.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - HEALTH AND PENSIONS.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
A difficult start to the year for German life insurers will not be made any better by the latest figures for private medical insurance, which stagnated in 1996.

The industry association put a brave face on things, arguing that sales are expected to pick up this year and noting that many people took out private medical insurance for the first time last year. The downside, as the figures show, is that an equal number of people did not renew existing cover.

This disappointing news for health insurers comes on top of concerns in three other areas affecting life insurers. Consumer representatives are questioning industry forecasts of returns on life policies, while watchdogs are clamping down on policies linked to home-loan repayments.

Thirdly, uncertainty rumbles on over possible payouts linked to Holocaust victims. While there is as yet no evidence to support suggestions that this will result in a huge payout, companies are keenly aware of the publicity implications of this delicate issue.
In Britain, by contrast, the outlook for life insurers continues to improve. Progress towards reforming the nation's pension system can be expected after May 1's election.

Whichever political party forms the next government, insurers expect to play a major role in pension provision. Each of the main parties has put forward its proposals and, although attention has focused on the differences, there are many similarities.

This is hardly surprising, since the same industry experts are often consulted by politicians of all hues. At least one leading firm of actuaries has links to both the Conservative and Labour parties.
People in the industry base their views on recent experience in other countries, with attention currently focusing on New Zealand's reform of its pension system.
British pension providers are likely to be in broad agreement with the proposed changes in New Zealand, which are based on individuals building up their own private retirement fund.
However, they may baulk at the prospect of New Zealand's true market forces solution, which rules out any tax relief on pension contributions.
